source.title: Primary School Curriculum Design — Agriculture, Grade 5 (First Published 2017, Revised 2024)
source.notes: Read directly from 'grade 5 designs/GRADE-5-AGRICULTURE-Curriculum-Designs.pdf' via the Read tool (no pages param), full text extracted, all 4 strands / 13 sub-strands / 120 lessons mined per CURRICULUM-MINING-GUIDE.md's 10-step checklist. Grade 5's official KICD title is 'Agriculture' alone (namesByGrade override in curriculum.ts), and the subject is an integrated agriculture + home science area (essence statement explicitly names clothing construction, laundry, and hygiene alongside crop/animal production).

subStrands.name: 1.1 Soil Conservation
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify sites for soil improvement in the school or community
Construct organic waste pit for soil improvement
Demonstrate use of plant remains for soil improvement
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we improve the soil using suitable organic wastes?
learningExperiences: Discuss and identify sites in the school or community that have poor soil for crop growth
Construct a pit, a site or a structure for dumping plant residue and suitable food remains and organic kitchen wastes in school
Plant crop in a residue pit to observe and appreciate soil improvement from accumulated organic wastes
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — construction and use of organic waste pit relates to waste management skills
coreCompetencies: Critical thinking and problem solving — observation skills identifying appropriate sites for soil improvement
subStrands.notes: No closed parenthetical list of organic waste types in the source (plant residue, food remains, kitchen wastes named as open examples) — implemented pool draws on these named examples.

subStrands.name: 1.2 Water Conservation
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify ways of conserving water for household gardening
Practice water conservation within the school or community
Appreciate importance of conserving water in the community
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we conserve soil water in household gardening practices?
learningExperiences: Use devices or other resources to search for information on ways of water conservation such as mulching, cover cropping and shading in kitchen and backyard gardening
Practise various ways of conserving water in farming (mulching, shading, cover cropping) within the school
Experiment mulching (mulch some crops and leave others un-mulched and compare moisture conservation)
Make presentations to share experiences on importance of conserving water (mulching, cover cropping and shading) in kitchen and backyard gardening activities
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — water conservation relates to knowledge of natural resources in the environment
coreCompetencies: Learning to learn — learning independently through self-driven water-conservation tasks
subStrands.notes: The mulching experiment (mulched vs un-mulched comparison) is explicit source content — good basis for an Analyze/Evaluate branch, not just recall of the 3 named methods.

subStrands.name: 1.3 Conserving Wild Animals
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify ways of repelling wild animals to avoid damage of property
Repel wild animals to avoid destruction of property
Appreciate importance of living better with wild animals
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we repel wild animals to avoid destruction of property?
learningExperiences: Watch video clips or listen to a resource person on safe ways of repelling wild animals (such as use of smoke, smells) to avoid damage on property (crops and domestic animals) and live better with wild animals
Innovate safe ways of repelling small wild animals (smoke, use of smell repellant or any other)
Discuss and make presentations on importance of conserving wild animals in the environment
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — conservation of wild animals relates to conservation of natural resources
coreCompetencies: Critical thinking and problem solving — evaluation and decision-making exploring ways of solving property destruction by wild animals
subStrands.notes: Critical thinking and problem solving named as a core competency — requires an Analyze/Evaluate branch (e.g. judging which repellent method suits a described situation), not just recall of method names. Source explicitly scopes to SMALL wild animals only ('innovate safe ways of repelling small wild animals') — large dangerous wildlife (elephants, buffalo) is out of scope for this sub-strand's practical/innovate outcome.

subStrands.name: 2.1 Growing Vegetables
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify gardening practices in growing vegetables
Establish a nursery bed for vegetables
Care for vegetable seedlings after transplanting
Appreciate the importance of vegetables in provision of healthy meals
keyInquiryQuestions: How does growing vegetables contribute to food production?
learningExperiences: Brainstorm and share experiences on gardening practices of vegetables in a nursery bed
Prepare a nursery bed (container or ground nursery), sow vegetable seeds and take care of the seedlings
Transplant vegetable seedlings and take care of the seedlings
Make class presentations on importance of growing vegetables as a source of food for animals and humans
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — growing vegetables relates to socio-economic activities in the community
subStrands.notes: Two-stage process (establish nursery bed → care for seedlings after transplanting) is a genuine sequence — good ordering-branch material.

subStrands.name: 2.2 Uses of Domestic Animals
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify uses of various domestic animals in food production processes
Relate various domestic animals to their uses
Appreciate the importance of domestic animals in food production
keyInquiryQuestions: How are domestic animals important in food production?
learningExperiences: Brainstorm and share experiences on the uses of domestic animals in food production (bees, rabbits, camels, fish, pigs, donkeys, dogs and cats)
Match domestic animals to their uses
Make class presentations on importance of domestic animals in various food production processes while relating contributions of all the scoped animals
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — rearing and uses of domestic animals as a socio-economic activity
scopeNotes: Note: 8 named domestic animals are an explicit, closed enumerated list — bees, rabbits, camels, fish, pigs, donkeys, dogs and cats — all 8 must be covered, including the non-obvious direct-food ones (bees=honey, rabbits/pigs=meat, camels=milk/meat, fish=food) and the indirect/non-food-product ones (donkeys=draught labour supporting farming, dogs=guarding livestock/property, cats=pest control protecting stored food) — the assessment rubric explicitly rewards 'relating contributions of all the scoped animals', so indirect contributions to food production count too, not just animals that are literally eaten or milked.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric/learning-experience explicitly says 'relating contributions of ALL the scoped animals' — this is a hard floor requiring all 8 named animals to be covered, not a representative sample.
coreCompetencies: Communication — speaking clearly making presentations on domestic animal uses
subStrands.notes: This is the clearest hard-floor enumerated pool in the whole Grade 5 Agriculture design — treat as non-negotiable, all 8 implemented with a genuine (not invented) use each.

subStrands.name: 2.3 Preservation of Cereals and Pulses
specificLearningOutcomes: Describe methods of preserving cereals and pulses in the locality
Preserve cereals and pulses for food security
Appreciate the importance of preserving cereals and pulses for food security
keyInquiryQuestions: How does preservation and storage of cereals and pulses enhance food security?
learningExperiences: Brainstorm and share experiences on methods of preserving and storing cereals and pulses (such as sun drying, use of ashes, use of airtight containers) at household level
Preserve and store cereals and pulses using methods such as sun drying, use of ash and airtight containers
Make class presentations to share experiences on importance of preserving and storing cereals and pulses
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — preservation of cereals and pulses relates to farming activities in the community
coreCompetencies: Critical thinking and problem solving — exploring ways of preserving/storing cereals and pulses to prevent spoilage
subStrands.notes: Critical thinking and problem solving named — needs an Analyze/Evaluate branch (choosing/judging the best preservation method for a described grain-spoilage scenario).

subStrands.name: 2.4 Food Nutrients
specificLearningOutcomes: Explain functions of food nutrients in the body
Categorise foods based on their major nutrients
Identify nutritional diseases and disorders associated with poor eating habits
Appreciate the importance of various nutrients in the body
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is the knowledge of food nutrients important in food production?
learningExperiences: Search and share information on functions of food nutrients (carbohydrates, vitamins, proteins, fats)
Use samples of food materials and photographs to categorise foods based on their major nutrients (protein rich foods, carbohydrates rich foods, vitamins and minerals rich foods)
Use print and digital devices to search for information on various nutritional diseases and disorders such as kwashiorkor, marasmus, goiter and anaemia
Make class presentations on the importance of various nutrients in the body
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — food nutrients relate to prevention of non-communicable diseases
coreCompetencies: Digital literacy — interacting with digital technologies searching for food-nutrient information
subStrands.notes: 4 nutrients, 3 food categories (note minerals folded into the vitamins category per source wording), 4 named disorders — all closed enumerated lists, hard floors.

subStrands.name: 2.5 Cooking Food
specificLearningOutcomes: Describe various methods of cooking food
Cook foods using various methods
Embrace dry fat frying and deep frying in food production
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we cook foods using dry fat frying and deep frying methods?
learningExperiences: Watch video clip or demonstration on dry fat frying and deep frying methods of cooking
Cook foods using dry fat frying and deep frying methods
Serve foods that have been cooked through dry fat frying and deep frying methods
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — safety and first aid from burns and scald
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Values box explicitly names 'observing safety as learners handle hot oils and equipment' — safety practice around hot fat/oil is part of the tested competency, not just the two frying methods themselves.
coreCompetencies: Learning to learn — self-discipline working cautiously to fry foods
subStrands.notes: Sub-strand header itself names exactly 2 methods (Dry Fat Frying, Deep Frying) — the closed pool for this sub-strand. Safety/burns-and-scald content is explicitly cross-linked, not incidental — worth its own evaluate-style branch.

subStrands.name: 3.1 Good Grooming Practices
specificLearningOutcomes: Describe good grooming as a daily health habit
Practice good grooming as a daily health habit
Appreciate good grooming as a healthy habit
keyInquiryQuestions: How does good grooming promote personal hygiene?
learningExperiences: Discuss and share experiences on aspects of good grooming (dressing and etiquette) for different occasions
Demonstrate different ways of dressing and etiquette for different activities
Conduct class modelling on different ways of dressing and etiquette to appreciate good grooming habits for different activities
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — good grooming habits relate to self-discovery
coreCompetencies: Self-efficacy — identification of self developing good grooming habits
subStrands.notes: Sub-strand header itself names exactly 2 aspects (Dressing, Etiquette) — the closed pool. 'For different occasions/activities' is explicit — implemented content should vary occasion/activity context (school, church, sports, formal visit, etc.), not give one generic rule.

subStrands.name: 3.2 Home Hygiene
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify surfaces made from different materials in home environment
Clean different types of surfaces in the home environment
Appreciate living in a clean home environment to promote healthy living
keyInquiryQuestions: How do you clean surfaces made from different materials?
learningExperiences: Discuss and share experiences on surfaces made from different materials such as glass, wooden, earthen floors, cemented and tiled
Clean different types of surfaces such as glass, wooden, earthen floors, cemented and tiled
Maintain cleanliness of surfaces in the school to appreciate living in clean environment
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — cleaning surfaces relates to preventing contamination and spread of communicable diseases
coreCompetencies: Communication and collaboration — listening/speaking skills using facts to support opinions in brainstorming
subStrands.notes: 5 named surface materials are an explicit closed list — each needs its own appropriate cleaning method (e.g. earthen floors are swept/smeared with dung-ash mixture traditionally, glass wiped, tiled/cemented mopped/scrubbed) matched correctly, not one generic 'clean it' answer for all 5.

subStrands.name: 3.3 Laundering Cotton Item
specificLearningOutcomes: Describe how to launder a cotton item
Launder a cotton item for personal hygiene
Appreciate importance of laundry work for hygiene purposes
keyInquiryQuestions: How does laundering cotton items promote hygiene?
learningExperiences: Watch a clip or observe a demonstration on how to launder a cotton item (white and fast coloured cotton)
Launder a white and fast coloured cotton item
Practice laundering of white and fast coloured items at home to appreciate the importance of laundry work for personal hygiene
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — personal hygiene relates to communicable diseases
coreCompetencies: Learning to learn — sharing ideas carrying out laundering activities with peers
subStrands.notes: White vs fast-coloured cotton need genuinely different handling (e.g. white can be bleached/boiled, fast-coloured must be washed separately in cool water to avoid running/fading) — 2-way distinction is the closed pool, not a single generic laundering procedure.

subStrands.name: 4.1 Repairing Garments
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify stitches used in repairing garment
Make samples of stitches used to repair garments
Use the stitches to repair gaping seam
Adopt the use of stitches to repair of garments
learningExperiences: Use pictures, samples of garments, video clips and charts to identify stitches such as back stitch and running stitch used in repairing garment
Make samples of running and back stitches
Use back stitch and running stitch to repair gaping seam
Make use of back stitch and running stitch to repair their daily wear
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — choice and use of colours relates to aesthetic skills
coreCompetencies: Critical thinking and problem solving — evaluation/decision-making exploring ways of repairing garment
subStrands.notes: Exactly 2 named stitches, both used specifically to repair a gaping seam — closed pool. Critical thinking and problem solving named — needs an Analyze/Evaluate branch (e.g. judging which stitch/approach suits a described torn-garment scenario).

subStrands.name: 4.2 Constructing Innovative Gardens
specificLearningOutcomes: Distinguish between horizontal and vertical innovative gardening
Construct innovative gardens for growing crops
Adopt the use of innovative gardens in growing crops
keyInquiryQuestions: How can gardening be done on vertical and horizontal spaces?
learningExperiences: Watch or observe stimulus materials (video clips, pictures and photographs) on innovative gardening practices to differentiate between vertical and horizontal gardens
Use sacks, plastic bottles, walls, plastic pipes among others to construct vertical and horizontal gardens for growing crops
Use the vertical and horizontal gardens to grow appropriate crop
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — designing structures and use of craft tools/equipment
coreCompetencies: Creativity and imagination — designing/assembling skills innovating vertical and horizontal gardens
subStrands.notes: 2 garden types × 4 named construction materials — the sack/vertical-tower and wall-mounted/plastic-bottle garden techniques should be correctly paired with horizontal vs vertical (e.g. sack/plastic-pipe/wall gardens are vertical; ground-level bed/tyre gardens are horizontal), not treated as interchangeable.
